sources.citation: Beckett, Patrick H. & Terry L. Corbett. 1992. The Manso Indians. Las Cruces: COAS Publishing and Research (47-page scan hosted by the BIA Office of Federal Acknowledgment as petition exhibit 005_PFWD_1992)
sources.note: Nothing on stress. p. 3: 'The first name applied to the Manso may have been Tanpachoas, a name used by Luxan in his journal of the Espejo expedition of 1582'. LANGUAGE section pp. 32-33: 'The Manso language is known from two words recorded in early Spanish sources and from seven words recorded by Bandelier in 1883.. Even their value for determining the phonetics of the language is practically nil'; the two words are arre 'yes' (Onate 1598) and ocae 'arrow' (Gallegos 1582); the Bandelier words are 'suspect'. p. 37: Troike (1988: 240) concluded Concho and Tanpachoa were Sonoran Uto-Aztecan.

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.3, languoid tanp1235 'Tanpachoa' (Unclassifiable; MX; 31.76/-106.49). Glottolog's most extensive descriptions: Troike 1988 (ref 306535) and Zamponi 2023 (ref 688660), both typed 'a wordlist or less'; ref 306535 language code note: 'Tanpachoa [NOCODE_Tanpachoa] attested in a couple of words each probably Sonoran affiliation'
sources.note: Nothing; no descriptive reference exists, only two 'a wordlist or less' comparative notes; language attested in a couple of words.

sources.citation: Hammond, George P. & Agapito Rey. 1966. The Rediscovery of New Mexico, 1580-1594. Albuquerque: University of New Mexico Press (Gallegos relation of the Chamuscado-Rodriguez expedition; Luxan's account of the Espejo expedition)
sources.note: Nothing; primary colonial attestation only. Gallegos, p. 79: 'These people call the arrow "ocae," the name given to bamboo by the Mexicans'; Luxan, p. 169: 'A large number of Indian men and women from another nation, called Tanpachoas, came to this place [Los Charcos del Canutillo]'; index: 'Tanpachoas.. see Mansos'.

sources.citation: Forbes, Jack D. 1957. The Janos, Jocomes, Mansos and Sumas Indians. New Mexico Historical Review 32(4): 319-334.
sources.note: No phonology content and no linguistic data at all. pp. 325-329 argue from Spanish colonial testimony (interpreters, alliances) that 'the Manso language was Athabascan' and that the Tanpachoa of 1582 lived opposite the Suma bank of the Rio Grande, against Sauer's and Scholes's Uto-Aztecan view; no words are cited.

sources.citation: Campbell, Thomas N. n.d. Tanpachoa Indians. Handbook of Texas Online. Austin: Texas State Historical Association.
sources.note: No phonology content. Only: 'The linguistic affiliation of the Mansos is still being debated. Some consider that it was Athapascan (Apache), others Uto-Aztecan.' Bibliography: Forbes 1959; Luxan (Hammond & Rey 1929); Newcomb 1961; Sauer 1934.

sources.citation: Seymour, Deni J. n.d. Manso/Tanpachoa. Web page, deni-seymour.com (archaeologist's research pages on protohistoric peoples of the southern Southwest).
sources.note: No phonology content, no words. Text: 'Manso (aka Tanpachoas, Gorretas) Not to be confused with the Manso Apache, the Manso of the El Paso/Cuidad Juarez area were Uto-Aztecan speakers. They were called Manso by Onate because they were considered peaceful, tame, or docile.' Remainder is archaeological/ethnohistorical.
